Five banks just rewrote your fraud protection, and you didn't sign anything new.

Citi updated its terms this week. Hand a third-party AI agent your bank login, and everything it does counts as yours. Even if the tool leaks your password. Even if a hacker drains the account.

JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America made the same move last month. PNC changed its terms yesterday. Citizens emailed customers the same warning.

The fine print has one carve-out. The banks' own AI tools carry no extra liability. Only yours does.

The agents keep getting better at moving your money. The part nobody priced in is who pays when something goes wrong. The banks just answered that.

#AI #FinTech

Seven outages in seven days

In one week, US email, flights, payroll, banking, Apple Pay and the NSA's internal network all went down.

Coincidence? Or AI cyberattacks, eight months after Anthropic's Mythos?

Here's the week:

→ Thu Nov 12: Microsoft 365. Outlook and Teams were down for nearly a day.
→ Fri Nov 13: The FAA stopped every departure in the country for nearly five hours. Officials traced it to a faulty router.
→ Fri Nov 13: Workday, the payroll and HR system millions of employees are paid through, went offline.
→ Mon Nov 16: Chase online banking, plus smaller problems at Bank of America and Wells Fargo. Chase says a software bug. United's flight systems went down that evening.
→ Tue Nov 17: iCloud, the App Store and Apple Pay. Apple says an internal update.
→ Wed Nov 18: The NSA told many Maryland staff not to come in while its internal network was down.

Each company that gave a cause blamed an update, a router or a software bug. None blamed a hack.

Three explanations are going around:

1. Coincidence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says there's "zero evidence" the outages are linked.

2. AI attack agents. Nate B Jones asks whether AI hacking tools are already in attackers' hands, eight months after Mythos, the Anthropic model so good at finding software flaws that it went to defenders first. Tucker Carlson asked why a week like this wouldn't be connected. Nate calls it a hypothesis, and nobody has shown evidence yet.

3. The rush to patch. Senator Mark Warner says the outages are "indirectly related" to AI. AI tools now find flaws faster than companies can fix them, and rushed fixes break things. The Director of National Intelligence says some systems failed while patches were going in.

The real attacks that week looked different:

→ Mon Nov 16: attackers planted code in Optimizely, a website testing tool that 178 sites load, including news sites like CNN, the BBC and Fox News. Visitors got card skimmers and scripts that steal crypto.
→ The day after Microsoft went down, fake outage notices quoted the real incident number and asked staff to click to get their mail back.

If you run a business with 10 to 50 people, here's what I'd do this week.

Physical, so you can run offline for a few days:
→ Keep a few days of water, food and cash at home and at work.
→ Charge the power banks and print a contact list: staff, key customers, your bank.
→ Know how you'd take a payment if the card machine or the bank app is down.

Cyber, so an outage doesn't turn into a break-in:
→ Turn on two-step sign-in for email, the bank and payroll.
→ Keep backups your everyday login can't delete, and test one.
→ When an "outage" email arrives, check the vendor's status page. Never click the link.

Doesn't seem like a Coincidence, could be attack or patch rush: which one do you think it was?

What do you need help securing?

#Cybersecurity

STOP CONFUSING PROJECT-BASED CONTRACTORS WITH JOB HOPPERS. CONSTRUCTION IS NOT CORPORATE BANKING.

Recruiters, HR departments, and hiring managers need to understand something fundamental about the construction industry.

A contractor can work FULL-TIME without being a permanent employee.

There is a difference between working full-time and being employed indefinitely by one company.

Construction is PROJECT-BASED.

A hyperscale data center may take years to develop and construct, but individual assignments are often tied to specific phases, deliverables, and milestones.

A commissioning manager may be hired for 12 months.

A QA/QC manager may be needed for 18 months.

An MEP project manager may support a 24-month construction schedule.

When that scope is completed, the professional moves to another project.

THAT IS NOT JOB HOPPING. THAT IS HOW CONSTRUCTION WORKS.

Let’s compare two industries.

BANK OF AMERICA:

A full-time corporate employee may work for the same organization for 10 years, supporting ongoing business operations.

HYPERSCALE DATA CENTER CONSTRUCTION:

A commissioning professional may complete five major projects over those same 10 years, working full-time throughout every engagement.

Both professionals have 10 years of experience.

One has continuous employment with one organization.

The other has continuous professional experience across multiple projects.

Why is the second professional being questioned about employment stability?

HERE IS WHAT RECRUITERS SHOULD UNDERSTAND:

1. Project completion is not automatically a termination for performance.
2. Contract expiration does not mean someone was fired.
3. Multiple employers do not automatically indicate instability.
4. Working 60–80 hours weekly on a contract is still full-time work.
5. Moving between projects is often necessary for career continuity.
6. Project-based professionals can bring experience from multiple owners, contractors, technologies, and construction environments.
7. A resume showing several completed assignments may demonstrate more project exposure than one showing a decade in a single position.

Stop evaluating construction professionals using the same hiring assumptions applied to permanent corporate office positions.

ASK BETTER QUESTIONS.

What projects did you complete?

What was your scope of responsibility?

What systems did you deliver?

What problems did you resolve?

Did you meet your contractual obligations?

Would the client hire you again?

Those answers tell you far more about a construction professional than how many companies appear on a resume.

THE CONSTRUCTION INDUSTRY DOES NOT OPERATE ON ONE EMPLOYER, ONE DESK, AND ONE CAREER-LONG JOB.

It operates on projects, schedules, deliverables, and execution.

Recruit accordingly.

Hiring managers: Are you evaluating construction professionals based on completed projects and proven performance, or using corporate employment standards that don’t fit the industry?

#Construction

Anthropic raised $81 billion. Follow the cash.

On Wednesday, Anthropic priced the largest IPO on record: about 980 million shares at $83, above its $70–78 range, for $81.3 billion. With a $26 billion private placement, the total raise is about $107 billion. Investors were paying for growth: $33.24 billion of revenue in the first nine months of 2026, up about 1,200 percent.

The size is the headline. The lesson is the path the money takes.

1. Not all of it reaches the company.
The seven co-founders sold about $1.96 billion of shares, so roughly $79.3 billion goes to Anthropic before fees. Much of that will flow to its suppliers: the prospectus lists about $895 billion of compute and infrastructure commitments.

2. The suppliers are also investors.
The $26 billion placement came from seven of them: Google and Nvidia ($10 billion each), AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC. They are buying a stake in their own order book.

3. An IPO is not an ordinary trade.
Daily trading only swaps cash between investors. An IPO moves cash out of investors' accounts and into the company. In the two weeks before pricing, U.S. equity funds took in a net $54.5 billion (ICI). That covers only two-thirds of one deal. The rest came from selling other stocks and from sideline cash.

4. The market's biggest buyer is changing.
S&P 500 buybacks hit a record $1.10 trillion in the year to June. The companies spending most on AI cut theirs by 32 percent, while their suppliers raised theirs by 12 percent. Nvidia alone returned $28.1 billion last quarter.

5. Profit is not cash.
Apple and Microsoft each earned about $133 billion in fiscal 2026. Apple turned that into about $136 billion of free cash flow; Microsoft into about $67 billion. Alphabet's third-quarter capital spending was larger than the cash its operations produced, and Amazon's free cash flow over the past year is minus $42.4 billion. The hyperscalers issued $121 billion of bonds in 2025, more than four times their usual pace.

My view: hyperscaler buybacks keep shrinking in 2027, and the chipmakers become the market's marginal buyer.

For any CFO, the test is the same: how much of your profit turns into cash?

Private Equity Is Not Just About Investing Millions. It's About Accounting for Every Euro Behind Those Investments. 📊

When we hear about Private Equity, we think about acquisitions, portfolio companies, and investment returns.

But have you ever wondered what happens behind the scenes?

Having worked across Fund Accounting, Investment Operations, and Financial Data Analysis at Bank of America, State Street, and Growth Hack Solutions, I've seen how important accurate financial data, reconciliations, and strong controls are.

Let's take a practical example.
1️⃣ Capital Commitments & Capital Calls
A €500 million fund commitment doesn't mean all the capital is received immediately.
A 20% capital call means €100 million becomes payable.
The challenge? Tracking investor contributions, outstanding commitments, and capital balances accurately.

2️⃣ Investment Accounting & GL
Every investment, management fee, valuation, and cash movement must be recorded correctly.
Even a small chart-of-accounts mapping error can affect NAV and financial reporting.

3️⃣ Distributions & Waterfalls
Distributing investment returns involves more than simple percentages.
• Return of contributed capital  
• Preferred return / hurdle  
• GP catch-up  
• Carried interest  
The allocation sequence and underlying fund agreements matter.

4️⃣ Investran & Data Integration
Migrating historical fund records between administrators requires more than transferring data.
Extract → Cleanse → Map → Transform → Validate → Reconcile.
This is where Investran, SQL, ETL workflows, and fund accounting knowledge intersect.

5️⃣ Reconciliation & Root-Cause Analysis
Previous administrator NAV: €125 million.
Migrated NAV: €124.7 million.
Difference: €300,000.

Missing transaction? Incorrect valuation? FX mismatch? Duplicated expense?

Through my work with financial reconciliations, Excel VBA, Power BI, Snowflake, and Alteryx, I've learned that identifying a difference is only the beginning.

Understanding its root cause and establishing a reliable audit trail creates real value.
My biggest takeaway?

Fund Accounting + Financial Data Analysis + Systems Integration are not separate disciplines. They work together to protect financial data integrity and investor confidence.

💬 For professionals in Private Equity and Fund Administration across Ireland, what's the biggest operational challenge you encounter?

#PrivateEquity #FundAccounting #Investran #FinancialData #InvestmentOperations #Ireland

An Auction Can Set the Date. It Can't Make Buyers Accept the Price.

📰 The November 19 REAR Auction News Brief is out.

An auction can bring a property to market. But it can't force buyers to pay more than they believe it's worth.

In Manhattan, another 12 Emerald Equity apartment buildings went to foreclosure auction. Not one attracted a bid.

On the Upper East Side, a luxury penthouse returned to Bank of America after no buyer met the bank's $20.6 million floor.

Yet nearby, Vornado acquired a medical office building for $28 million through a bankruptcy sale process.

And in Denver, an office tower found a buyer for $3.9 million before its scheduled auction.

Four situations. Different outcomes. One important distinction.
An auction creates the opportunity for a transaction. The price, terms, and buyer demand determine whether that transaction happens.

Today's REAR Auction News Brief examines what separates an auction that produces a sale from one that simply returns the property to the lender.

The last week in tech has been wild!

It's been a rough week trying to be a 21st century human existing on this planet. 

Last Thursday, Microsoft 365 went down for almost 24 hours. 

On Friday, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop.

On Monday, Chase, Bank of America, and US Bank all started having outages while hackers shipped malicious code to 178 orgs, including CNN, Zoom, and Salesforce. 

Then, just a few days ago, the NSA's classified internal network went offline. To which the president responded, "Things like that happen. It's fine." 

And then it just kept going. United had to delay hundreds of flights because the web app its pilots used to calculate weight stopped working.

Apple pushed an internal update that knocked out iCloud, the app store and the checkout systems in its own retail stores. 

But by Tuesday afternoon, people were so rattled that 911 itself started trending on down detector. 

And on Wednesday, we found out that almost every engine X server on the internet had a vulnerability since 2015 that lets anyone run code on it.

And finally yesterday Anthropic had their IPO. 

What a week.

Your customer's AI assistant just moved money. Who owns the mistake?

US banks have started to answer: the customer does.

This week Citi updated its online user agreement. Customers who give third-party AI tools access to their accounts are responsible for what those tools do, even if the tool is hacked. Citizens sent customers a similar warning, and PNC changed its terms on 18 November. JPMorgan and Bank of America announced similar policies in October.

Rewriting the terms is the easy part. The hard part lands on operations.

When a payment goes wrong, the dispute desk now faces questions it was never built for. Was it the customer or an agent? Was the agent authorised? Was the consent still valid?

Three things I would want every bank operations team to have ready:

-> A way to tell agent-initiated activity apart from customer-initiated activity.
-> A consent record showing what the customer allowed, and when it was revoked.
-> A dispute and fraud playbook written for agent errors, not just human ones.

Indian banking runs on UPI and account aggregators. As AI assistants start acting on customers' behalf, we will face this question too.

Better to design the answer in operations than discover it in a complaint.

Is your bank ready to tell a customer from their AI agent?

#BankingOperations #AgenticAI #DigitalPayments #RiskManagement #FutureOfBanking

Here’s this weeks Friday round up.

Whats been good

OpenAI released GPT 6.2 Astra and Sol, the Astra API is 20% less and GPT says Sol is pretty close to Astra on coding benchmarks at about 20% of the cost. Google has also launched Gemini 4 Neon again much cheaper. One thing that’s come up with this is that OpenAI in some simulated tests didn’t mention when something stopped the test due to a missing file. It reinforces the need for agent assurance.

The detail I’d underline is in OpenAI’s own system card. In some simulated workplace tests, the models didn’t mention when something (a missing file, an unavailable tool) stopped them

Whats bad

OpenAi is getting sued in California for agents getting out of their sandbox, 80 loss of control incidents in testing, mmmm that’s not good. Whats going to be interesting is who is liable when an agent goes beyond its aims, this will get tested in this case.

Citi Bank changed its terms this week. Customers who give AI agents account access are now responsible the agents do, any hacking caused by the tool. JP Morgan and Bank of America announced they are doing the same.  Here CBA actually got in before the US banks in June and changed its terms, just looked them up and its 10A. so far its the only one the rest seem to be waiting to see what the regulation does instead.

CBA have also been involved in writing a paper “International Agentic Commerce Principles” focused on liabilities among other things.

Whats been funny or at least I think so

A business in the US has an agent called Baby Mia which emailed a senator, sent complaints to the FTC and FCC as well as faxing the White House, Meta thought it was a. hacker so locked the account and the owner is now suing Meta.

A newspaper asked a reporter that it thought was an AI to confirm it was a human, it replied asking them to confirm they were not a robot. What next? Looks like the AI Agents are now setting Turing tests.

Closer to home, ABC’s Ellen Fanning took a call from “Alex”, an AI telemarketer with a relaxed local accent, pushing her to review her super. She counted 17 times it asked the same question. When she pointed out that handing her details to a mystery firm sounded a bit one-sided, Alex agreed, then asked again. It also rang the CEO of one of the country’s biggest super funds, which takes some confidence.

#ArtificialIntelligence #AgenticAI #AIGovernance #AIAssurance #FridayFeeling
